title: How to Waterproof Cinder Block Walls: Test, Prep, Then Seal
h1: How to Waterproof Cinder Block Walls
query: how to waterproof cinder block walls
description: Tape foil to the block for 24 to 48 hours first: seepage needs a masonry waterproofer scrubbed in 2 coats; rain-soaked exterior block needs a silane-siloxane.
dek: Tape foil to the block for 24 to 48 hours first: seepage needs a masonry waterproofer scrubbed in 2 coats; rain-soaked exterior block needs a silane-siloxane.
intro: Block is hollow, porous and laced with mortar joints, so the right sealer depends on where the water comes from. Test the wall first, then match the product to the side it faces.

To waterproof a cinder block wall, first tape a square of foil to it for 24 to 48 hours to see whether the water is condensation or seepage, then match the sealer to the side the water comes from. A wall that seeps from wet soil needs a masonry waterproofer scrubbed into bare block; a wall soaked by rain needs a penetrating repellent. Below: testing, prep, products and limits.

quickAnswer: The best way to seal cinder blocks to avoid moisture is to work in order: find out what kind of water you have, fix the outside water sources, clean and patch the block, then apply the one product family that suits the wall. Interior basement block that seeps gets a cement-and-latex masonry waterproofer brushed hard into bare block. Above-grade exterior, garage and garden walls get an invisible silane-siloxane repellent. The steps below take most homeowners two or three weekends, largely because of drying time.

sections.h: Is a Wet Cinder Block Wall Condensation or Seepage?

blocks.p: Run the foil test before you buy any cinder block sealant, because the answer decides whether you need a sealer at all. Tape a piece of aluminum foil or clear plastic, about a foot square, flat against the bare block with all four edges sealed by duct tape. Leave it for 24 to 48 hours, then peel it off and look at both sides.

blocks.h3: How do you read the foil test?

blocks.p: Moisture on the room side of the foil is condensation: warm, humid basement or garage air hitting cool block and dropping its water, the same way a cold glass sweats in summer. No sealer fixes that, because the water never came through the wall. A dehumidifier set to around 45 to 50 percent humidity, better air circulation and insulating cold surfaces are the cure, and our guide on [how to fix a damp basement](/how-to-fix-a-damp-basement/) walks through them.

Moisture under the foil, on the block side, means water is moving through the wall from the soil or from wet cores inside the block. That is seepage, and it is the case where a cinder block wall sealer earns its money. If both sides are wet, you have both problems, which is common in summer, and you should treat them together: seal the wall and run a dehumidifier.

blocks.h3: What signs point to water inside the block cores?

blocks.p: Block walls give you clues that poured concrete does not. A dark, damp band along the bottom one or two courses after rain usually means the hollow cores have filled with water that is draining down inside the wall. White, powdery efflorescence on the mortar joints shows that water is travelling through the wall and leaving its dissolved salts behind as it evaporates. Damp patches that appear in the same squares every storm often trace one leaky core or a cracked face shell.

Timing helps too. Wetness only in muggy weather, never after rain, is condensation. Wetness within a day of a downpour is seepage. Water running along the floor edge points to the wall-slab joint, which no coating can seal.

sections.h: Should You Seal Cinder Block From the Inside or the Outside?

blocks.p: Seal the side the water hits first whenever you can reach it. On an above-grade wall, a garage, or the exposed face of a garden wall, that is the outside face, and a penetrating sealer there stops rain from soaking in. On a basement block foundation, the water side is buried, so most homeowners waterproof the inside face and fix drainage outside instead of digging.

blocks.h3: Why is waterproofing the outside better engineering?

blocks.p: A membrane on the soil side of a foundation keeps water from ever entering the block, so the hollow cores stay dry and the wall never carries water to the inside. On an existing house it means excavating to the footing, so it is usually reserved for walls that need structural repair or sit in long-term saturated soil.

blocks.h3: When is sealing the inside enough?

blocks.p: Interior sealing works when the water pressure behind the wall is modest: damp patches, slow seepage and a dark band after storms, especially once gutters and grading have been fixed. It is the practical choice for most block basements, and the right product to seal basement wall inside house is a cement-based masonry waterproofer, not ordinary paint or a clear sealer.

Interior sealing is not enough when water flows out of the wall, pools at the floor edge, or keeps pushing coatings off. Then the wall needs drainage, not a thicker coat. For the full drainage sequence, from downspouts to drain tile, see our guide on [how to waterproof a basement](/how-to-waterproof-a-basement/); this page stays with the block wall itself.

blocks.h3: Masonry waterproofing coatings

blocks.p: These are the products most people mean by basement sealer. They go on like very thick paint, fill the pinholes and pores of the block face, and cure to a hard, paint-like film. Makers rate them for a stated hydrostatic pressure; DRYLOK Extreme, for example, is rated by its manufacturer to withstand 15 psi. They need bare, clean masonry to bond, and they change the look of the wall, though most come in white and can be tinted. This is the answer to the best sealer for a wet basement wall.

blocks.h3: Silane and siloxane repellents

blocks.p: Penetrating repellents soak into the block and leave it looking unchanged. Siloxanes handle the large surface pores of block well, silanes reach deeper, and blends of the two are the usual choice for masonry; our comparison of [silane vs siloxane sealers](/silane-vs-siloxane-sealers/) covers the chemistry. They excel at stopping rain and splash, which reduces freeze-thaw damage and efflorescence, but they are not designed to hold back water pushed through a wall from wet soil, and many leave a surface that paint will not grip.

blocks.h3: Silicate densifiers

blocks.p: Silicate sealers, sold as sodium, potassium or lithium silicates and by brands such as RadonSeal, react with lime and calcium compounds inside concrete to form a gel that blocks the capillaries. They leave nothing on the surface, so there is nothing to peel. They work best on dense poured concrete with plenty of reactive material and somewhat less predictably on lean, hollow block, and they only react with bare, unsealed masonry.

blocks.h3: Clear acrylic sealers

blocks.p: Acrylics form a thin clear film that can darken the block slightly or add a sheen. They are popular for decorative split-face block, but on a wall that takes on water from behind, the film can trap moisture, whiten and peel. They are a cosmetic choice for dry, sheltered walls rather than a waterproofing method.

sections.h: What Is the Best Water Sealer for Cinder Blocks on Each Wall?

blocks.p: The best water sealer for cinder blocks is the one that matches where the wall sits and which side the water comes from. Our ranked list of the [best cinder block sealers](/best-cinder-block-sealer-reviews/) names specific products in each family; here is how to choose the family for each kind of block wall around a house.

blocks.h3: Basement block foundations

blocks.p: Inside a basement, the water arrives from the soil side, so choose a masonry waterproofer rated for hydrostatic pressure and scrub it into bare block in two coats. A penetrating repellent is an option only for a wall that is merely damp and that you want to leave unpainted. If the wall is wet enough that water drips or flows, coat it only after drainage has been addressed. Our guide to the [best basement wall sealers](/best-basement-wall-sealer/) sorts products by how much water each can handle.

blocks.h3: Garage and exterior above-grade walls

blocks.p: Rain, splash and, in cold regions, road salt carried in on cars are the threats here. A silane-siloxane repellent sprayed onto the exterior face keeps block from soaking up water and salt and leaves it looking natural. Inside a garage, a block wall that only gets splashed at the bottom can be treated the same way, or painted with a masonry paint system if you want color. If appearance is the goal, our guide to the [best paint for cinder block](/best-paint-for-cinder-block/) covers block filler and topcoats.

blocks.h3: Garden walls, retaining walls and planters

blocks.p: These walls take water from both sides: rain on the face and wet soil behind. The back of a retaining wall should have been waterproofed with a membrane and drained with gravel and a pipe when it was built. On an existing wall, a repellent on the exposed face and the top course helps, but efflorescence and staining will continue while the soil behind stays wet, so make sure any weep holes along the base are open and not buried.

blocks.h3: Is a clear acrylic sealer good for exterior cinder block walls?

blocks.p: For most people asking for the best exterior clear acrylic sealer for cinder block walls, a clear penetrating silane-siloxane is the better buy, because it leaves no film to whiten or peel and lets the block breathe. Choose a water-based acrylic only for a dry, sheltered decorative wall where you want a sheen or a deeper color, and expect to recoat it more often than a penetrating sealer.

sections.h: How Do You Prep Cinder Block Before Sealing?

blocks.p: Prep decides whether any cinder block sealant works, because penetrating sealers must soak in and coatings must bond to bare masonry. Paint, old sealers, efflorescence, dust and mildew all block both.

blocks.h3: How do you remove efflorescence?

blocks.p: Dry-brush the white deposits with a stiff nylon or wire brush first, since many of the salts come off dry. Then clean with a masonry cleaner or an efflorescence remover made for concrete, following its dilution and safety instructions, and rinse thoroughly. Acid cleaners need gloves, eye protection and ventilation. If the white crust returns within weeks, water is still moving through the wall, and that needs fixing first.

blocks.h3: Should you strip paint from block before sealing?

blocks.p: Yes, for nearly every product. A penetrating sealer cannot reach the block through a paint film, and a masonry waterproofer is usually labeled for bare masonry only. Splash water on the wall: where it darkens and soaks in, the block is ready; where it beads, something is already on the surface and must come off by wire brushing, grinding or a masonry stripper.

blocks.h3: How do you patch holes and active leaks with hydraulic cement?

blocks.p: Hydraulic cement is the standard fix for open holes, tie holes and spots where water is actively trickling through. Chisel the hole out into an undercut shape, wider at the back than at the face, about three quarters of an inch deep or more. Mix a small batch stiff, press it in with a gloved hand, and hold it until it sets, which takes only minutes. It expands as it sets, which locks it into the hole and stops the flow.

blocks.h3: What about mortar joints and open cores?

blocks.p: Rake out loose or crumbling mortar and repoint with fresh mortar or a masonry patch, then let it cure for the time on the bag; fresh mortar is alkaline, and some coatings ask you to wait before applying. Check the top course of a block foundation as well. If the cores are open under the sill plate, water and air can enter the wall from above, and they should be capped with solid block, mortar or foam.

sections.h: How Do You Apply Sealer to a Cinder Block Wall?

blocks.p: Application depends on the product family, and the two methods are nearly opposites. Coatings are scrubbed in and built up in layers; penetrating sealers are flooded on and allowed to soak. In either case, read the label's temperature window, usually above 40 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, and wait for a dry forecast on exterior walls.

blocks.h3: Applying a masonry waterproofer to basement block

blocks.p: Stir the product thoroughly, since the solids settle. Using a stiff nylon brush made for masonry coatings, scrub the first coat hard into the block, working it into every pinhole, mortar joint and the joint where the wall meets the floor slab as far as you can reach. A roller skips the voids in block, and each pinhole left behind is a path for water. Let the first coat dry for the time on the label, then apply a second coat; a brush or a thick-nap roller usually works for the second coat once the pores are filled.

Coverage drops on block. DRYLOK lists roughly 75 to 100 square feet per gallon for the first coat on smooth masonry, and rough or split-face block takes more. Buy for two full coats, and buy a little extra rather than stretching the product thin.

blocks.h3: Applying a penetrating repellent to exterior block

blocks.p: Use a low-pressure pump sprayer and work from the bottom of the wall upward so the run-down saturates the block below. Many makers call for a flood coat, enough product to create a run-down of several inches below the spray line. On porous block a second coat, often applied wet-on-wet, is common; follow the label's timing. Back-brush rough block and mortar joints to push the sealer into the texture, and protect glass, plants and painted trim from overspray.
SAFETY
Ventilate, and treat solvent sealers as flammable.

Open windows and run a fan to exhaust air when coating a basement. Wear gloves, eye protection and a respirator rated for the product. Keep solvent-based sealers away from pilot lights, furnaces and water heaters, and use a sturdy ladder for the top courses of tall walls.
After curing, splash-test a repellent-treated wall; water should bead. On a coated wall, hold a flashlight flat to the surface to find pinholes and dab them with more product.

sections.h: When Can a Sealer Not Stop a Leaking Block Wall?

blocks.p: No basement water leakage sealant can win against steady hydrostatic pressure. When the soil around a foundation stays saturated, water presses against the outer face shell, fills the cores and pushes at the inner face. A good coating slows it, but heavy pressure blisters and peels coatings, and the water then appears at the floor edge instead. The cure is reducing the water, not adding layers.

blocks.h3: Start with gutters, downspouts and grading

blocks.p: Most block basement leaks start with roof water dumped at the foot of the wall. Clean the gutters, extend every downspout so it discharges several feet from the foundation, and rebuild soil so it slopes away from the house. These cheap jobs often turn a seeping wall into a damp one a coating can handle.

blocks.h3: Interior drain tile and weep holes for block

blocks.p: When water keeps entering at the floor joint, a contractor installs an interior perimeter drain: a trench along the footing with perforated pipe running to a sump pump. On block foundations, installers commonly drill small weep holes into the bottom course so the water held in the hollow cores drains into the new system, which a solid poured wall does not need. A dimpled membrane on the wall often directs any seepage down into the trench.

blocks.h3: Cracks that need an engineer, not a sealer

blocks.p: Stair-step cracks through mortar joints, horizontal cracks along a course, or any inward bow in a block wall indicate soil pressure on the structure. Sealing them hides the evidence while the force keeps working. Have a structural engineer look before you coat, since the fix might be wall anchors, bracing or rebuilding a section.

mistakes: Sealing a block wall that only sweats does nothing, because condensation forms on the room side of the block. Tape foil or plastic to the wall for a day or two before buying anything. If the moisture is on the room side, a dehumidifier and better air movement solve the problem for far less money than a sealer.
Rolling the first coat onto block

A roller bridges the pinholes and voids in block instead of filling them, and each one becomes a path for water. Scrub the first coat of any masonry waterproofer into the wall with a stiff brush, working the product into mortar joints, then roll or brush the second coat once the pores are closed.

The white salt crust and old paint both stop a sealer from bonding or soaking in, and the new coat will flake off with them. Brush and clean efflorescence away, strip paint, and splash-test the wall. Any area where water still beads instead of darkening the block needs more prep.
Using a repellent against soil water

Silane-siloxane repellents shed rain beautifully on exterior block, but they are not built to stop water pushed through a basement wall from saturated soil. On the inside of a seeping basement wall, use a masonry waterproofer rated for hydrostatic pressure and fix gutters and grading outside first.
Coating a cracked or bowing wall

Stair-step cracks, horizontal cracks and inward bowing in block are signs of soil pressure on the structure, not just a water path. A fresh coating hides them while the force keeps working. Have a structural engineer inspect the wall before you seal it, since the repair may need anchors or bracing.
bottomLine: Waterproofing a cinder block wall starts with the foil test and the gutters, not the sealer. Once you know the water is coming through the block, clean off efflorescence and paint, patch leaks with hydraulic cement, repoint bad joints, and then choose by side: a masonry waterproofer scrubbed into interior basement block, a silane-siloxane repellent on exterior, garage and garden walls. If a coated wall blisters, water pools at the floor edge, or the block shows stair-step or horizontal cracks, stop sealing and look at drainage or structure instead. For specific products in each family, see our [cinder block sealer reviews](/best-cinder-block-sealer-reviews/).

faqs.q: What is the best way to seal cinder blocks to avoid moisture?
faqs.a: Find the water source first with a foil test, then fix gutters and grading outside. On a basement wall that seeps, scrub two coats of a masonry waterproofer into bare, clean block. On exterior, garage or garden walls hit by rain, spray on a silane-siloxane repellent. Clean off efflorescence and paint before either, and patch active leaks with hydraulic cement.

faqs.q: What type of sealer is best for waterproofing cinder block?
faqs.a: It depends on the side the water comes from. Cement-and-latex masonry waterproofers, the Drylok-type products, suit interior basement block because they resist water pressure to a labeled rating. Silane-siloxane penetrating repellents suit exterior above-grade block. Silicate densifiers are best on bare poured concrete, and clear acrylics are mainly cosmetic for dry, sheltered walls.

faqs.q: Do silicate sealers work on basement walls?
faqs.a: Silicate sealers work by reacting with lime inside bare concrete, so they suit clean, unpainted poured walls best and perform less predictably on hollow block. They will not react through paint, old sealers or a layer of dirt and dust, so scrub and rinse the wall first. They reduce dampness but are not designed to stop heavy seepage from saturated soil.

faqs.q: What product seals a basement wall from inside the house?
faqs.a: A cement-based masonry waterproofer brushed onto bare block is the standard interior product. Makers rate these coatings for hydrostatic pressure; DRYLOK Extreme, for example, is rated by its manufacturer for 15 psi. Hydraulic cement handles active leaks and holes before coating. Ordinary latex paint, clear acrylics and repellents are not substitutes on a seeping basement wall.

faqs.q: Can you waterproof cinder block from the inside only?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Interior sealing handles dampness and slow seepage well once roof water and grading are under control, and it avoids excavation. It cannot stop water entering at the joint between wall and floor or hold back heavy pressure. If coatings blister or water pools along the floor after storms, the wall needs interior drain tile or exterior work.

faqs.q: How long does a sealed cinder block wall stay waterproof?
faqs.a: Labels on silane-siloxane repellents commonly quote around five to ten years in typical exposure, and interior masonry waterproofers usually last a similar period before touch-ups. Sunny, wet exterior walls wear faster than sheltered ones. Splash water on a repellent-treated wall each year; when it soaks in instead of beading, clean the wall and reapply.

faqs.q: Can you paint over a sealed cinder block wall?
faqs.a: It depends on the sealer. Masonry waterproofers are designed to be the finish or to take a latex topcoat after they cure, and most come in tintable colors. Many silane-siloxane repellents leave a surface that paint will not grip, so check the data sheet before sealing. If you want color, choose a waterproofer or a block filler and masonry paint system instead.
